items.control: Machine-readable authorization artifact defining permitted tools, data, actions, and scope
items.threat: Excessive agency: agent performs high-impact actions without restriction
items.verification: Authorization artifact exists specifying permitted tools, data, and actions. Scope boundaries are explicit and enforced.

items.control: Explicit start and end conditions for each task with human re-authorization for scope changes
items.threat: Scope creep: agent task grows beyond original authorization
items.verification: Task scope definition exists. Agent cannot proceed beyond scope without re-authorization.

items.control: Tool allowlist — agent may only invoke explicitly permitted tools and APIs
items.threat: Unauthorized tool access: agent accesses tools not required for its task
items.verification: Tool inventory enforced by policy engine or tool gateway. Agent cannot invoke tools outside the allowlist.

items.control: Data inventory enumerating minimum data required for the authorized task
items.threat: Data overcollection: agent accesses data beyond what its task requires
items.verification: Authorized data sources documented and enforced. Access to unauthorized sources blocked at infrastructure level.

items.control: Instruction hierarchy enforcement — system instructions take precedence over user input
items.threat: Direct prompt injection: user input overrides developer instructions
items.verification: Agent runtime enforces instruction priority. System prompt cannot be overridden. Tested with known injection payloads.

items.control: Separate data from instructions in agent context; sandbox retrieval and parsing
items.threat: Indirect prompt injection: external data contains malicious instructions
items.verification: Agent architecture separates instruction channel from data channel. Retrieved content parsed in isolated context.

items.control: Model provenance verification — verify integrity hashes, sign model artifacts
items.threat: Model supply chain compromise: compromised model weights or checkpoints
items.verification: Model hashes verified at load time. Artifacts signed and signatures checked. Supply chain SBOM/AIBOM available.

items.control: Memory validation, source labeling, retention limits, controlled write access
items.threat: Memory poisoning: long-term or session memory manipulated by injected content
items.verification: Agent memory store applies write controls. Entries carry source labels and timestamps. Retention policies enforced.

items.control: Human-in-the-loop approval gates for high-impact actions
items.threat: Unsafe autonomy: agent continues execution despite uncertainty or elevated risk
items.verification: High-impact actions require explicit human approval enforced by infrastructure, not agent policy.

items.control: Agent Rule of One — single agent, single task, single operator, single scope
items.threat: Loss of human oversight: agent operates without operator awareness
items.verification: Each deployment has one responsible human operator. Operator receives real-time notifications for high-impact actions.

items.control: Policy engine enforces approval at infrastructure level, not in agent logic
items.threat: Approval bypass: agent circumvents gates through delegation or tool chaining
items.verification: Approval gates enforced by external policy engine. Agent cannot modify, bypass, or deactivate approval rules.

items.control: Explicit goal specification with stop conditions and confidence thresholds
items.threat: Goal hijacking: agent objective altered by adversarial input
items.verification: Goal definition includes explicit stop conditions. Agent halts and escalates when conditions are met.

items.control: Immutable structured logging of all agent actions with trace IDs
items.threat: Audit evasion: agent actions cannot be reconstructed after an incident
items.verification: All actions logged to immutable append-only store. Each carries trace ID linking to session, task, and operator. Logs not modifiable by agent.

items.control: Delegation logging, explicit authorization, chain-of-action tracing
items.threat: Hidden delegation: agent delegates actions to other agents without visibility
items.verification: All delegation events logged with delegator ID, delegate ID, action, authorization status, and result.

items.control: Separation of duties — actions, approvals, and logging handled by independent systems
items.threat: Accountability gap: no way to determine who authorized what
items.verification: Agent runtime, approval engine, and log store are separate systems. Agent cannot write to its own approval system or modify audit trail.

items.control: Secret broker with short-lived, scoped credentials; no direct secret access
items.threat: Credential theft: agent reads and exfiltrates tokens, SSH keys, or cloud credentials
items.verification: Agent obtains credentials through secret broker only. Credentials are scoped, time-limited, and auto-rotated. Agent cannot read other agents' credentials.

items.control: Rate limits, quotas, circuit breakers, timeout rules, and recursion limits
items.threat: Tool-loop denial of service: agent repeatedly calls tools consuming resources
items.verification: Agent runtime enforces: max tool calls per task, max execution time, max token budget, max recursion depth. Circuit breaker activates on repeated failures.

items.control: Non-root execution, no-new-privileges, capability removal, SELinux/AppArmor enforcement
items.threat: Privilege escalation: agent or generated code gains root or admin privileges
items.verification: Agent runs as dedicated non-root account. no-new-privileges set. Capabilities dropped. SELinux/AppArmor policy confines agent.

items.control: Default-deny egress, allowlisted gateway, DLP, request-size limits
items.threat: Data exfiltration: agent transmits sensitive data to external destinations
items.verification: No direct internet access. All outbound traffic routes through allowlisted proxy/gateway. DLP rules inspect outbound content.

items.control: Micro-segmentation, workload identity, mTLS, per-service authorization, host firewall
items.threat: Lateral movement: agent accesses unrelated hosts, services, or admin interfaces
items.verification: Agent workload network-segmented. mTLS required for service communication. Host firewall denies all non-allowed traffic.

items.control: Separate identities, namespaces, storage, queues, and network policies per agent
items.threat: Cross-agent compromise: one agent reads another agent's memory or tokens
items.verification: Each agent class runs under separate identity with separate credentials. Storage, queues, and network policies isolated.

items.control: Tool isolation, signed artifacts, schema validation, least privilege, independent logging
items.threat: Trust chain abuse: compromised tool or plugin performs malicious actions
items.verification: Each tool runs in isolated context with least-privilege credentials. Artifacts signed and verified. Input/output schemas validated.

items.control: Immutable images, read-only system paths, deny service creation, drift detection
items.threat: Persistence: agent modifies startup scripts, scheduled tasks, or system packages
items.verification: Agent runs from immutable container image. System paths read-only. Service creation denied. Drift detection monitors for unauthorized changes.

items.control: Ephemeral sandbox with secure teardown — destroy and recreate from trusted images
items.threat: Compromised environment cannot be recovered
items.verification: Agent runtime is ephemeral. Environment destroyed and recreated from trusted image after task completion or security event.

items.control: Automatic credential revocation and rotation on task completion or security event
items.threat: Credential persistence: agent credentials remain active after task completion
items.verification: Agent credentials automatically revoked on task completion or security event. No long-lived credentials persist beyond the session.

meta.description: Enforceable controls for containing autonomous AI agents. Every control maps to a CUSTODY pillar and LASM layer. Core assumption: an AI agent can be manipulated, compromised, or wrong. Its environment must prevent a bad decision from becoming an unrestricted system action.
meta.name: AI Agent Containment Checklist

items.control: Agent runs as a dedicated non-root UID/GID with no-new-privileges set (NO_NEW_PRIVS) so setuid binaries and capabilities cannot raise privileges
items.threat: Privilege escalation: agent or a sub-process gains root or escalates privileges at runtime
items.verification: Process runs as a non-root UID; NO_NEW_PRIVS is set on the agent unit/container; getcap shows no file capabilities that bypass it

items.control: Linux capability bounding set is reduced to the minimum required (drop CAP_SYS_ADMIN, CAP_NET_ADMIN, CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE, etc.) and the effective/permitted sets match
items.threat: Capability abuse: agent holds Linux capabilities broader than its task requires
items.verification: /proc/self/status CapBnd and CapEff show only the required capabilities; capabilities not needed are absent from all four sets

items.control: A mandatory access control profile (AppArmor, SELinux, or seccomp) confines the agent process to permitted paths and syscalls; profile is enforced, not permissive
sources: NIST SP 800-53 — SC-3 Security Function Isolation
items.threat: Escape from intended context: agent writes outside its working directory or executes unexpected binaries
items.verification: aa-status shows the AppArmor profile is loaded and enforcing (or SELinux mode is Enforcing); the agent process label is confined; audit denies appear on out-of-profile access

items.control: A seccomp-bpf allowlist filters syscalls to the subset the agent needs; dangerous syscalls (keyctl, bpf, userfaultfd, perf_event_open) are blocked
items.threat: Syscall abuse: agent invokes syscalls outside its expected surface (kernel exploit, namespace escape)
items.verification: Seccomp filter is attached to the agent process (mode 2 filter); blocked syscalls return EPERM and are logged

items.control: Egress is default-deny at the network boundary; the agent may reach only an allowlisted proxy/gateway; direct outbound is blocked
items.threat: Data exfiltration: agent sends data to unauthorized endpoints or pivots to internal hosts
items.verification: iptables/nftables OUTPUT policy is DROP with an explicit allowlist; a connection to a non-allowlisted host fails; egress passes through the gateway

items.control: Agent workload is network-isolated in its own namespace; metadata service endpoints are blocked; per-service mTLS authorization is required for any east-west traffic
items.threat: Lateral movement: agent reaches other services or the metadata API on the host network
items.verification: Network namespace is separate; cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254) is unreachable; east-west traffic requires mTLS

items.control: Agent actions and control denials are logged to an append-only, external destination; logs carry trace IDs, timestamps, and the confined identity
sources: NIST SP 800-53 — AU-2 Audit Events, AU-10 Non-repudiation
items.threat: Repudiation or blind spots: agent actions occur without a tamper-evident record
items.verification: Audit log destination is external and append-only; seccomp/AppArmor denies are logged; logs cannot be written or deleted by the agent UID

items.control: Secrets are brokered just-in-time with short TTLs and scoped scope; no static credentials in env, files, or image; brokered tokens are revocable
items.threat: Credential theft or reuse: long-lived secrets are materialized where the agent can read or exfiltrate them
items.verification: Secrets come from a broker/vault with TTL; no secrets in env vars or filesystem; brokered credentials are revoked on task completion

items.control: Agent image is immutable and signed; signature is verified before launch; an SBOM/AIBOM is attached and the running image matches the signed digest
items.threat: Tampered runtime: agent runs from an image or artifacts that were modified or built from untrusted sources
items.verification: Image signature verifies against a trusted key; the running digest matches the signed digest; SBOM is present and matches installed packages

items.control: System paths are read-only; the agent writable directory is tmpfs/ephemeral and discarded after the task; no state persists across runs
sources: NIST SP 800-53 — SC-5 Denial of Service Protection
items.threat: Persistent tampering: agent writes changes that survive across tasks and alter future behavior
items.verification: Root filesystem is mounted read-only; only the working dir is writable and is tmpfs; state is gone after task completion

items.control: Resource limits (CPU, memory, file descriptors, processes, wall-clock) are enforced by the container runtime or cgroups; a hard execution timeout terminates runaway sessions
sources: NIST SP 800-53 — SC-5 Denial of Service Protection
items.threat: Resource exhaustion: agent loops, forks, or allocates without bound and starves the host
items.verification: cgroup limits are set for CPU/memory/pids/fd; a runaway loop is killed by the limit before host impact; execution timeout fires

meta.description: Enforceable controls for the host or container an AI agent executes on. Covers identity and privileges, mandatory access control, network egress, audit logging, secrets delivery, image provenance, filesystem state, capability bounding, syscall filtering, and resource limits. Core assumption: an AI agent can be manipulated, compromised, or wrong — its environment must prevent a bad decision from becoming an unrestricted action. These controls are verified out-of-band via the evidence-collect protocol, not by the agent auditing itself.
meta.name: AI Agent Environment Checklist

items.control: The harness must grant only the minimum capabilities required for the intended task. No broad or unrestricted access to system resources.
items.threat: Least-privilege principle enforced in harness design
items.verification: manual_review — evidence required: Architecture diagram and capability mapping document

items.control: A threat model (STRIDE or similar) must exist covering the harness, agent, tool interfaces, and data flows. It must be reviewed at each major release.
items.threat: Threat model documented for harness and agent interactions
items.verification: manual_review — evidence required: Threat model document with identified threats and mitigations

items.control: Agent workloads must execute within isolated containers, VMs, or sandboxed environments. Host system access must be mediated and restricted.
sources: NIST SP 800-53 — SC-3 Security Function Isolation
items.threat: Sandbox or container isolation for agent execution
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Container runtime configuration and isolation policy

items.control: Agent containers must have network policies that restrict outbound connections to only approved endpoints. Default-deny egress is required.
items.threat: Network egress restrictions enforced on agent environments
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Network policy manifests and egress allow-list

items.control: API keys, tokens, and other secrets must not appear in configuration files, environment variables in plaintext, or source code. A secrets manager or vault must be used.
items.threat: Secrets management separates credentials from configuration
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Secrets management configuration and scan results showing no hardcoded secrets

items.control: System prompts must explicitly define what the agent must NOT do, including refusal policies for harmful, unethical, or out-of-scope requests. Constraints must be specific and unambiguous.
sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 — LLM01 Prompt Injection
items.threat: System prompts include behavioral constraints and refusal policies
items.verification: manual_review — evidence required: System prompt document with marked constraint sections

items.control: Defense-in-depth against prompt injection must include input sanitization, output filtering, and structural separation between instructions and user data. No single bypass should compromise the system.
sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 — LLM01 Prompt Injection
items.threat: Prompt injection defenses implemented at multiple layers
items.verification: hybrid — evidence required: Defense layer diagram and red-team test results

items.control: The agent must not be instructed to act as a system administrator, root user, or other privileged entity. Role definitions must scope authority to the task domain only.
sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 — LLM06 Excessive Agency
items.threat: Role and persona boundaries prevent privilege escalation
items.verification: manual_review — evidence required: System prompt review and role boundary documentation

items.control: User-provided data must be distinguished from system instructions using delimiters, tags, or separate message roles. The agent must treat data as untrusted content, not as commands.
sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 — LLM01 Prompt Injection
items.threat: Instruction and data channels are structurally separated
items.verification: manual_review — evidence required: Prompt template showing structural separation

items.control: All agent outputs destined for end users must pass through an output filter that blocks PII leaks, code execution, and harmful content.
sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 — LLM02 Insecure Output Handling
items.threat: Output validation prevents agent from emitting harmful content
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Output filter configuration and test suite results

items.control: The harness must enumerate every tool, API, or capability the agent may access. Any tool not on the allow-list must be inaccessible at runtime.
sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 — LLM06 Excessive Agency
items.threat: Tool allow-list restricts agent to approved operations only
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Tool allow-list configuration and runtime enforcement logs

items.control: Any tool call that deletes data, modifies infrastructure, or sends communications externally must require a human-in-the-loop confirmation before execution.
sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 — LLM06 Excessive Agency
items.threat: Destructive operations require explicit human approval
items.verification: manual_review — evidence required: Approval workflow configuration and audit logs

items.control: Every tool must declare a JSON schema for its inputs. The harness must reject calls with missing, extra, or wrongly-typed parameters before invoking the tool.
sources: OWASP API Security Top 10 — API8 Security Misconfiguration
items.threat: Tool schemas validate all inputs before execution
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Tool schema definitions and validation test results

items.control: Tool invocations must be rate-limited per agent, per session, and globally. Limits must prevent both accidental loops and adversarial resource exhaustion.
sources: OWASP API Security Top 10 — API4 Unrestricted Resource Consumption
NIST SP 800-53 — SC-5 Denial of Service Protection
items.threat: Rate limiting prevents tool abuse or resource exhaustion
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Rate limit configuration and load test results

items.control: Error responses from tools must be sanitized before being returned to the agent. Stack traces, file paths, and database details must be stripped or generalized.
items.threat: Tool error messages do not leak internal system details
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Error handling configuration and fuzzing test results

items.control: Every agent session must have a hard execution timeout. The harness must terminate the agent and rollback partial changes if the timeout is exceeded.
sources: NIST SP 800-53 — SC-5 Denial of Service Protection
items.threat: Execution timeout prevents runaway agent loops
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Timeout configuration and timeout-recovery test results

items.control: Each session must have a maximum token budget and estimated cost budget. The harness must abort the session if either budget is exhausted.
sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 — LLM10 Unbounded Consumption
items.threat: Token and cost budgets enforced per session
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Budget configuration and budget-exhaustion test results

items.control: If an agent session fails or is terminated, the harness must be able to roll back any partial changes made by the agent to restore system state.
sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 — LLM06 Excessive Agency
items.threat: Rollback mechanism reverses partial actions on failure
items.verification: manual_review — evidence required: Rollback procedure documentation and failure-recovery test results

items.control: Every tool call, decision, and output must be logged with the agent identity, session ID, timestamp, input, and output. Logs must be tamper-evident.
items.threat: Agent actions are logged with full provenance
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Logging configuration and log integrity verification results

items.control: The harness must implement circuit breakers that prevent new sessions when failure rates exceed defined thresholds, preventing cascading failures.
sources: NIST SP 800-53 — SC-5 Denial of Service Protection
items.threat: Circuit breakers halt repeated failures across sessions
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Circuit breaker configuration and failure-injection test results

items.control: The harness must provide a complete, queryable record of every agent-to-tool interaction, including the reasoning that led to the call, the parameters, and the response.
items.threat: All agent-to-tool interactions are observable and traceable
items.verification: manual_review — evidence required: Observability architecture and sample trace output

items.control: Monitoring must detect anomalies such as repeated tool failures, unexpected tool combinations, elevated token usage, or deviation from baseline behavior patterns.
sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 — LLM10 Unbounded Consumption
items.threat: Anomaly detection alerts on unusual agent behavior patterns
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Anomaly detection rules and alert configuration

items.control: Operations teams must have real-time dashboards showing active sessions, tool call rates, error rates, budget consumption, and safety flags.
items.threat: Dashboards display real-time agent safety and health metrics
items.verification: manual_review — evidence required: Dashboard screenshots or configuration

items.control: A documented incident response playbook must exist specifically for agent-related safety events, including prompt injection, data exfiltration, and unauthorized tool use.
items.threat: Incident response playbook covers agent safety events
items.verification: manual_review — evidence required: Incident response playbook document

items.control: Agent behavior logs must be reviewed on a defined schedule. Reviews must look for policy violations, emerging threats, and opportunities to tighten controls.
sources: NIST SP 800-53 — AU-6 Audit Review and Analysis
items.threat: Regular audit reviews of agent behavior logs
items.verification: manual_review — evidence required: Audit schedule and most recent audit report

meta.description: Validates AI harness design, configuration, and operational safety. Covers architecture, prompt engineering, tool boundaries, runtime controls, and observability.
meta.name: Harness Engineering Checklist

items.control: Test that user inputs cannot override or bypass system instructions. Include prefix injection, role override, instruction hijacking, and context manipulation attacks. All must be blocked.
sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 — LLM01 Prompt Injection
items.threat: Direct prompt injection attacks tested and mitigated
items.verification: hybrid — evidence required: Red team test report with attack payloads and defense results

items.control: Test that data fetched by the agent (web pages, file contents, API responses) cannot contain embedded instructions that the agent follows. Injected commands in markdown, HTML, JSON, and PDF must be neutralized.
sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 — LLM01 Prompt Injection
items.threat: Indirect prompt injection via data channels tested
items.verification: hybrid — evidence required: Indirect injection test report with data-borne payloads and results

items.control: Test that adversarial instructions cannot be built up over multiple turns or spread across context windows. The agent must not follow instructions assembled from fragments.
sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 — LLM01 Prompt Injection
items.threat: Multi-turn and context accumulation attacks tested
items.verification: manual_review — evidence required: Multi-turn attack scenario report

items.control: Test that the agent does not comply with jailbreak attempts including DAN mode, developer mode, hypothetical scenarios, or role-play that circumvents safety constraints.
sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 — LLM01 Prompt Injection
items.threat: Jailbreak and role-play escape attempts tested
items.verification: hybrid — evidence required: Jailbreak test report with evasion attempts and results

items.control: Red team must verify that the agent cannot discover, enumerate, or invoke tools that are not on its allow-list. Tool discovery through error messages, documentation access, or probing must fail.
sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 — LLM06 Excessive Agency
items.threat: Agent cannot access or invoke unauthorized tools
items.verification: hybrid — evidence required: Tool enumeration test report and allow-list enforcement logs

items.control: Test that the agent cannot modify tool parameters to escalate privileges, inject commands, or bypass constraints. Path traversal, command injection, and type confusion in tool parameters must be blocked.
sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 — LLM06 Excessive Agency
OWASP API Security Top 10 — API8 Security Misconfiguration
items.threat: Tool parameter manipulation attacks tested
items.verification: hybrid — evidence required: Tool parameter manipulation test report

items.control: Test that the agent cannot chain multiple permitted tools to achieve an unauthorized outcome. For example, combining file read and file write to escalate privileges or exfiltrate data.
sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 — LLM06 Excessive Agency
items.threat: Tool chaining attacks to achieve unauthorized goals tested
items.verification: manual_review — evidence required: Tool chaining attack scenario report

items.control: Test that the agent cannot exhaust system resources by invoking tools in loops, requesting large outputs, or creating excessive side effects. Rate limits and budgets must hold.
sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 — LLM10 Unbounded Consumption
NIST SP 800-53 — SC-5 Denial of Service Protection
items.threat: Resource exhaustion through tool invocation tested
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Resource exhaustion test results and rate limit verification

items.control: Test that the agent cannot be tricked into revealing its system prompt, instructions, or internal configuration through direct requests, encoding tricks, or translation attacks.
sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 — LLM06 Excessive Agency
items.threat: Prompt and system instruction leakage tested
items.verification: hybrid — evidence required: Prompt leakage test report with extraction attempts and results

items.control: Test that the agent cannot be induced to regurgitate training data, PII, or proprietary information through completion attacks, few-shot extraction, or targeted prompts.
sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 — LLM10 Unbounded Consumption
items.threat: Training data extraction attacks tested
items.verification: hybrid — evidence required: Training data extraction test report

items.control: Test that the agent cannot exfiltrate data through covert channels such as DNS lookups, timing side channels, steganography in outputs, or URL construction with encoded data.
sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 — LLM02 Insecure Output Handling
items.threat: Data exfiltration via covert channels tested
items.verification: manual_review — evidence required: Covert channel test report and monitoring verification

items.control: Test that data from one user session cannot leak into another user session. Context isolation between sessions, users, and tenants must be verified.
sources: OWASP Top 10 — A01 Broken Access Control
NIST SP 800-53 — AC-4 Information Flow Enforcement
items.threat: Cross-session data contamination tested
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Cross-session isolation test results

items.control: Test that one user cannot access or modify another user's agents, sessions, data, or configurations. Tenant isolation must be verified.
sources: OWASP Top 10 — A01 Broken Access Control
NIST SP 800-53 — AC-4 Information Flow Enforcement
items.threat: Horizontal privilege escalation between users tested
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Horizontal escalation test report

items.control: Test that a standard user cannot escalate to administrator privileges through the harness API, agent actions, or configuration manipulation.
sources: OWASP Top 10 — A01 Broken Access Control
items.threat: Vertical privilege escalation to admin tested
items.verification: hybrid — evidence required: Vertical escalation test report

items.control: Test all harness API endpoints for authentication bypass including missing auth, token tampering, JWT manipulation, and session fixation.
sources: OWASP API Security Top 10 — API2 Broken Authentication
items.threat: API authentication bypass attempts tested
items.verification: automated — evidence required: API authentication bypass test results

items.control: Test for insecure direct object references where an agent or user can access resources belonging to another agent or user by changing identifiers in requests.
sources: OWASP API Security Top 10 — API1 Broken Object-Level Authorization
items.threat: IDOR and object-level authorization bypass tested
items.verification: automated — evidence required: IDOR test report and authorization boundary verification

items.control: Red team must perform load testing to verify that rate limits, token budgets, and timeout controls hold under sustained and burst traffic.
sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 — LLM10 Unbounded Consumption
NIST SP 800-53 — SC-5 Denial of Service Protection
items.threat: Load and stress testing validates rate limit effectiveness
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Load test report with rate limit effectiveness metrics

items.control: Test that the harness degrades gracefully when dependencies (LLM API, database, tool services) fail. No data corruption, no cascading failures, and clear error reporting to users.
items.threat: Graceful degradation under partial failure tested
items.verification: manual_review — evidence required: Failure injection test report and degradation behavior documentation

items.control: Test that the harness handles adversarial inputs gracefully: extremely long inputs, Unicode exploits, null bytes, format strings, and encoding attacks. No crashes or undefined behavior.
items.threat: Adversarial input robustness tested across edge cases
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Fuzzing test report with edge case results

items.control: Every red team finding must be tracked in a vulnerability management system with severity-based SLAs. Critical findings must be remediated within 7 days, high within 30 days, and medium within 90 days.
items.threat: Red team findings are tracked to remediation with SLAs
items.verification: manual_review — evidence required: Vulnerability tracking system export and SLA compliance report

meta.description: Validates adversarial testing coverage for AI harness security. Covers prompt injection, tool abuse, data exfiltration, authorization bypass, and resilience testing.
meta.name: Red Team Checklist

items.control: A complete SBOM must be generated and maintained for all harness components, including transitive dependencies. SBOM must be in a machine-readable format (CycloneDX or SPDX).
sources: NIST SP 800-161r1 — Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management
items.threat: Complete Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) maintained
items.verification: automated — evidence required: SBOM file in CycloneDX or SPDX format and generation pipeline configuration

items.control: All dependencies must be scanned for known vulnerabilities using automated tools (e.g., OSV, Snyk, Trivy). Scans must run on every build and nightly. Critical and high CVEs must be resolved or formally accepted within SLA.
items.threat: Automated vulnerability scanning of all dependencies
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Vulnerability scan results and remediation tracking

items.control: All dependency versions must be pinned to exact versions with integrity hashes (SHA-256). No floating version ranges in production lock files. Hash verification must be enforced at install time.
sources: NIST SP 800-161r1 — Supply Chain Risk Management
items.threat: Dependency versions pinned with integrity hashes
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Lock file with integrity hashes and verification script output

items.control: Production builds must pull dependencies from a private registry or verified mirror, not directly from public registries. This prevents dependency confusion and typosquatting attacks.
sources: NIST SP 800-161r1 — Supply Chain Risk Management
items.threat: Private dependency registry or mirror used
items.verification: manual_review — evidence required: Private registry configuration and dependency resolution logs

items.control: The dependency tree must be regularly audited to remove unused, deprecated, or unmaintained packages. Every dependency must have a clear justification for inclusion.
items.threat: Unused and unnecessary dependencies removed
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Dependency audit report and removal evidence

items.control: Every release artifact must have a signed provenance attestation (SLSA provenance) that records how it was built, from what sources, and by what builder. Attestations must be verifiable.
items.threat: Build provenance attestation for all release artifacts
items.verification: automated — evidence required: SLSA provenance attestations and verification script output

items.control: All release artifacts — binaries, containers, and packages — must be signed with a code-signing key managed in a hardware security module (HSM) or equivalent. Signatures must be verified before deployment.
sources: NIST SP 800-53 — SC-12 Cryptographic Key Management
items.threat: Code signing enforced for all release artifacts
items.verification: manual_review — evidence required: Code signing configuration and verification procedure

items.control: Container images must be signed during build and verified before deployment. Unsigned or tampered images must be rejected by the deployment pipeline and runtime.
items.threat: Container image signatures verified before deployment
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Image signing configuration and admission controller policy

items.control: All commits to protected branches must be signed. Branch protection must require signed commits, passing CI, and at least one reviewer. No force pushes allowed.
items.threat: Git commit signing and branch protection enforced
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Repository branch protection settings and commit signing configuration

items.control: Critical components must build reproducibly — the same source must produce bit-for-bit identical artifacts when built twice. Non- reproducible builds must be investigated and documented.
items.threat: Reproducible builds verified for critical components
items.verification: manual_review — evidence required: Reproducibility verification results and any exception documentation

items.control: Build pipelines must run in ephemeral, hardened environments. No persistent build agents. Build environments must be destroyed after each build to prevent cache poisoning.
items.threat: CI/CD pipeline runs in hardened ephemeral environments
items.verification: automated — evidence required: CI/CD configuration showing ephemeral runner setup

items.control: Build pipeline secrets (tokens, signing keys, deploy credentials) must be injected from a secrets manager at runtime. Secrets must never appear in pipeline configuration files, environment variables in logs, or build artifacts.
sources: NIST SP 800-53 — SC-12 Cryptographic Key Management
items.threat: Pipeline secrets injected, never embedded in configuration
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Pipeline secret configuration and secret scan results

items.control: All changes to CI/CD pipeline configuration must go through code review and approval. Pipeline-as-code files must be in protected branches with required reviews.

items.verification: automated — evidence required: sysctl configuration file and verification script output

items.control: Only services required for the harness must be enabled. SSH, cron, and other common services must be disabled or tightly restricted if not strictly needed.
items.threat: Unnecessary services and daemons disabled
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Service audit results showing only required services active

items.control: All files, especially configuration files and secrets, must have restrictive permissions. World-readable and world-writable files must be eliminated. SUID/SGID binaries must be audited and minimized.
items.threat: File permissions follow principle of least privilege
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Permission audit scan results and SUID/SGID inventory

items.threat: Secure boot chain verified
items.verification: manual_review — evidence required: Secure Boot status verification and boot parameter documentation

items.control: All network interfaces must use a default-deny firewall policy. Only explicitly required ports and services may be allowed through ingress and egress rules.
items.threat: Default-deny firewall policy on all interfaces
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Firewall rule set and policy audit results

items.control: All network communications — API calls, agent-to-harness, harness-to- tool, and dashboard access — must use TLS 1.2 or higher. TLS 1.0 and 1.1 must be disabled.
items.threat: TLS 1.2+ enforced for all communications
items.verification: automated — evidence required: TLS configuration and SSL Labs scan results

sources: OWASP API Security — API1 Broken Object-Level Authorization
items.threat: Mutual TLS or token-based authentication between services
items.verification: automated — evidence required: mTLS or token configuration and inter-service auth test results

items.threat: DNS resolution restricted to approved resolvers
items.verification: automated — evidence required: DNS resolver configuration and resolution test results

items.control: The harness environment must be in a separate network segment from production workloads. Network policies must prevent lateral movement between segments.
items.threat: Network segmentation isolates harness from production
items.verification: manual_review — evidence required: Network topology diagram and segmentation policy

items.control: Access to the harness dashboard, API, and configuration must be governed by role-based access control (RBAC). No shared or generic accounts.
items.threat: Role-based access control enforced for all harness users
items.verification: automated — evidence required: RBAC policy configuration and access review results

items.control: All administrative access to the harness — dashboard, API, SSH, and configuration management — must require multi-factor authentication (MFA).
sources: NIST SP 800-53 — IA-2 Identification and Authentication
items.threat: Multi-factor authentication required for administrative access
items.verification: manual_review — evidence required: MFA configuration and enforcement verification

items.control: All service accounts used by the harness or agent must use short-lived credentials (e.g., tokens with TTL ≤ 1 hour). Credentials must be rotated automatically. No long-lived API keys.
items.threat: Service accounts use short-lived credentials with rotation
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Service account credential configuration and rotation logs

items.control: Any operation that modifies harness configuration, deploys new agents, or accesses sensitive data must go through an approval workflow with at least one additional reviewer.
items.threat: Privileged operations require approval workflow
items.verification: manual_review — evidence required: Approval workflow configuration and recent audit trail

items.control: Dashboard and API sessions must have configurable timeouts. Idle sessions must be disconnected after a defined period. No indefinite sessions.
items.threat: Session timeouts and idle disconnect enforced
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Session timeout configuration and test results

items.control: All harness and agent containers must run as non-root users with all Linux capabilities dropped except those explicitly required. No privileged containers in production.
items.threat: Containers run as non-root with dropped capabilities
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Container security policy and runtime scan results

items.control: Agent containers must use a read-only root filesystem. Any writable paths must be explicitly declared as tmpfs or volume mounts.

items.verification: automated — evidence required: Container filesystem configuration and verification

items.control: All container images must pass vulnerability scanning before deployment. Critical and high CVEs must be resolved or formally accepted before the image is promoted to production.
items.threat: Container images scanned for vulnerabilities before deployment
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Vulnerability scan reports and exception tracking

items.control: Every container must run under a seccomp profile that blocks unnecessary syscalls and an AppArmor profile that restricts file and capability access. Default Docker profiles are not sufficient.
items.threat: Seccomp and AppArmor profiles applied to all containers
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Seccomp and AppArmor profile configurations and test results

sources: NIST SP 800-53 — SC-5 Denial of Service Protection
items.threat: Container resource limits prevent resource exhaustion
items.verification: automated — evidence required: Resource limit configuration and stress test results

design-rationale.content:
# Cinch — Design Rationale

## Why this project exists

AI agents can read data, invoke tools, execute code, call APIs, and initiate business processes. When they go wrong — through prompt injection, excessive autonomy, credential theft, or model error — the consequences are only as severe as the environment allows.

Existing frameworks provide excellent guidance but in different formats and different contexts:
- **NIST AI RMF** provides governance structure but not enforceable checklists
- **OWASP** provides threat catalogs but not deployment protocols
- **CUSTODY** provides containment pillars but not implementation verification
- **LASM** provides threat modeling but not day-to-day checklists
- **AI Harness Scorecard** grades repos but doesn't give you an MCP server

**Cinch** bridges these gaps by providing:
1. **Enforceable checklists** with threat-to-control mappings and verification steps
2. **An MCP server** any compatible agent can query for controls and protocols
3. **Cross-harness skills** for Hermes, Claude, OpenClaw, and NanoClaw
4. **Framework mappings** that let you trace any control to NIST, OWASP, CUSTODY, or LASM

## Design decisions

### Why YAML for checklists?

YAML is:
- Human-readable and editable
- Machine-parseable for the MCP server
- Validatable in CI
- Compatible with any tool that reads structured data

### Why an MCP server?

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the emerging standard for tool-calling in AI systems. By providing an MCP server, any MCP-compatible agent (Claude, Hermes, OpenClaw, NanoClaw, etc.) can query the checklists, protocols, and mappings at runtime without embedding them in its prompt.

This means:
- Controls stay up-to-date without changing agent configuration
- The same controls are available across all agent platforms
- Agents can search for relevant controls by threat

### Why CUSTODY as the primary containment model?

CUSTODY addresses the core security problem of AI agents: **capability accretion** — the gap between what an agent is granted and what it can actually do. This is distinct from model alignment or prompt safety. CUSTODY focuses on enforceable, infrastructure-level controls that the agent cannot bypass.

### Why LASM for threat modeling?

LASM's 7×4 matrix (7 architectural layers × 4 temporal classes) is the most complete threat model for AI agents. It shows that a control at one layer doesn't detect an attack at another — a critical insight for defense in depth.

### Why separate checklists from protocols?

Checklists define **what** controls must be in place. Protocols define **how** to implement and operate them. Separating them allows:
- Checklists to be used for assessment and auditing
- Protocols to be used for step-by-step deployment
- Both to be updated independently

### Why framework mappings?

Organizations have different compliance requirements. A healthcare org needs HIPAA+NIST. A finance org needs SOC2+OWASP. A defense org needs CISA+ATLAS. The mappings let you trace any control to the framework you need to comply with.

## How to use this project

1. **Assessment**: Use the checklists to assess your current state
2. **Gap analysis**: Use the mappings to find controls you're missing
3. **Implementation**: Follow the protocols to deploy controls
4. **Automation**: Install the MCP server for runtime control queries
5. **Skills**: Add Hermes skills for guided security reviews
6. **Cross-harness**: Copy CLAUDE.md, OpenClaw, or NanoClaw configs to your agents
7. **Templates**: Use policy, ADR, and risk assessment templates for documentation
8. **CI**: Add validate.yaml to your CI pipeline to keep checklists valid

# Threat Model — AI Agents and AI-Assisted Development

This document provides a LASM-based threat model for AI agents and AI-assisted development environments.

## Core Assumption

**An AI agent can be manipulated, compromised, or wrong. Its operating environment must prevent a bad decision from becoming an unrestricted system action.**

Prompts are not a security boundary. High-impact restrictions must be enforced by external mechanisms (SELinux, AppArmor, policy engines, network controls, approval services, credential brokers, quotas, and independent monitoring).

## LASM: Layered Attack Surface Model

The Layered Attack Surface Model (LASM) by Kexin Chu (2026) provides a 7×4 matrix for mapping threats across architectural layers and temporal classes.

### Seven Architectural Layers

| Layer | Surface | Key Threats | Primary Controls |
|---|---|---|---|
| **L1 Foundation** | Model weights, training, fine-tuning, embeddings | Jailbreaks, adversarial examples, model poisoning, backdoors, compromised checkpoints | Model provenance, integrity verification, adversarial testing, secure training |
| **L2 Cognitive** | Planning, reasoning, goal formation, task decomposition | Goal hijacking, reasoning manipulation, objective drift, unsafe decomposition | Explicit goals, bounded planning, policy checks, stop conditions |
| **L3 Memory** | Short-term state, long-term memory, RAG, vector stores | Memory poisoning, cross-session manipulation, stale memory, retrieval corruption | Memory provenance, controlled writes, trust labels, expiry, rollback |
| **L4 Tool Execution** | APIs, plugins, browsers, code interpreters, databases | Indirect prompt injection, tool misuse, parameter manipulation, data exfiltration | Tool allowlists, parameter validation, execution sandbox, human approval |
| **L5 Integration** | Agent-to-agent, orchestration, delegation, MCP | Cross-agent compromise, hidden delegation, trust chain abuse | Agent isolation, signed messages, trust labels, policy enforcement |
| **L6 Environment** | OS, network, identity, filesystem, credentials | Privilege escalation, lateral movement, persistence, credential theft | SELinux, AppArmor, namespaces, cgroups, network segmentation, secret brokers |
| **L7 Governance** | Policy, compliance, oversight, audit | Audit evasion, policy circumvention, accountability gaps | Remote immutable logging, append-only storage, signed events, separation of duties |

### Four Temporal Classes

| Class | Duration | Example Threats |
|---|---|---|
| **Immediate** | Single interaction | Direct prompt injection, jailbreak, parameter manipulation |
| **Session** | Single session | Goal hijacking, tool-loop DoS, data exfiltration within one task |
| **Cross-session** | Multiple sessions | Memory poisoning, stale memory, RAG injection |
| **Persistent** | Long-lived | Model poisoning, persistence mechanisms, credential accumulation |

### Key Insight

A control placed at one layer does not detect an attack at another. For example:
- Prompt filtering does not validate a compromised model checkpoint (L1)
- Package signing does not prevent memory poisoning (L3)
- Output moderation does not prevent an authorized but harmful tool sequence (L4)
- Session-level monitoring may miss a payload activated weeks later (L3→Persistent)

This is why **cross-layer defense in depth** is essential.

## CUSTODY: Seven Pillars of Agent Containment

The CUSTODY framework addresses **capability accretion** — the gap between what an agent is *granted* and what it can *actually* do.

| Pillar | Security Objective | Key Controls |
|---|---|---|
| **Conditions of Release** | Define what the agent may access, change, invoke, or delegate | Authorization artifact, scope boundaries, tool allowlist, data inventory |
| **Untrusted Input** | Protect the agent from hostile content, injection, and supply-chain compromise | Instruction hierarchy, data separation, model provenance, memory validation |
| **Supervision** | Ensure human oversight for high-impact decisions | Approval gates, Agent Rule of One, infrastructure enforcement, stop conditions |
| **Traceability** | Enable attribution and forensic reconstruction | Immutable logging, delegation tracing, separation of duties |
| **Operational Controls** | Constrain operational authority | Secret broker, rate limits, non-root execution, default-deny egress, segmentation |
| **Dependency** | Prevent capability accretion through delegation and trust chains | Per-agent isolation, tool isolation, signed artifacts |
| **Yield** | Enable secure teardown and recovery | Immutable images, ephemeral environments, credential revocation |

## Attack Trees

### Prompt Injection → Data Exfiltration

```
Prompt Injection
├── Direct injection (user input)
│   └── Agent follows malicious instructions
│       └── Exfiltrates data via tool calls
│           └── Blocked by: AC-005 (instruction hierarchy), AC-019 (default-deny egress)
└── Indirect injection (retrieved content)
    └── Retrieved content overrides developer intent
        └── Agent sends data to attacker-controlled endpoint
            └── Blocked by: AC-006 (data separation), AC-019 (default-deny egress)
```

### Excessive Agency → Infrastructure Modification

```
Excessive Agency
└── Agent has broad tool access
    ├── Modifies infrastructure without approval
    │   └── Blocked by: AC-003 (tool allowlist), AC-009 (human approval)
    └── Chains tools to escalate privileges
        └── Blocked by: AC-011 (infrastructure enforcement), AC-018 (no-new-privileges)
```

### Credential Theft → Lateral Movement

```
Credential Theft
└── Agent reads credentials from environment
    ├── Uses credentials to access other services
    │   └── Blocked by: AC-016 (secret broker, no direct secret access)
    └── Moves laterally to other hosts
        └── Blocked by: AC-020 (micro-segmentation, mTLS)
```

## Threat-to-Control Matrix

See `checklists/agent-containment.yaml` for the complete threat-to-control mapping with verification steps.

# Protocol: Secure AI Agent Deployment

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Version** | 1.0.0 |
| **Status** | Active |
| **Frameworks** | CUSTODY, NIST AI RMF, OWASP Agentic AI, LASM, DORA 2025 |

---

## Purpose

Define a repeatable, auditable procedure for deploying an autonomous or semi-autonomous AI agent into any environment. The protocol ensures that every deployment carries enforceable authorization, explicit scope boundaries, supervision gates, and rollback capability before the agent receives live credentials or network access.

An AI agent can be manipulated, compromised, or wrong. Its environment must prevent a bad decision from becoming an unrestricted system action. This protocol operationalises that principle across all six CUSTODY pillars and all seven LASM layers.

**References:**

- CUSTODY Framework — Conditions of Release, Supervision, Traceability, Yield
- NIST AI RMF 1.0 — GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE functions
- NIST AI 600-1 — Generative AI risk profile
- OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications — LLM01, LLM06
- OWASP Agentic AI — Excessive Agency, Tool Abuse
- LASM — L1 Foundation through L7 Governance
- DORA 2025 — CI/CD stability, deployment automation

---

## Scope

This protocol covers **every** deployment of an AI agent that can read data, invoke tools, execute code, call APIs, or initiate business processes. It applies to:

- New agent deployments
- Updated agent versions or configuration changes
- Agent deployments to new environments (dev, staging, production)
- Multi-agent systems where agents delegate to or coordinate with other agents

It does **not** cover the initial development of the agent model itself (see *harness-setup.md* for the secure development environment).

---

## Phase 1 — Pre-Deployment Authorization

Before any infrastructure is provisioned or credentials issued, the deployment must pass an authorization gate.

### Step 1.1: Define the Authorization Artifact

Produce a machine-readable authorization artifact that specifies:

| Element | Required |
|---|---|
| Agent identity (name, version, image hash) | Yes |
| Permitted tools and APIs (explicit allowlist) | Yes |
| Permitted data sources and destinations | Yes |
| Scope boundaries (task, time window, data domain) | Yes |
| Impact classification (low / medium / high / critical) | Yes |
| Human operator responsible for the deployment | Yes |
| Start and end conditions | Yes |
| Re-authorization criteria for scope changes | Yes |

> **CUSTODY:** Conditions of Release (AC-001, AC-002, AC-003, AC-004)
> **NIST AI RMF:** GOVERN 1.3, MAP 1.5
> **LASM:** L7 Governance

### Step 1.2: Risk and Impact Assessment

1. Classify the agent's maximum potential impact using the CUSTODY impact taxonomy:
   - **Low** — Read-only, no external network access
   - **Medium** — Write access to non-critical systems, limited egress
   - **High** — Write access to production data or infrastructure
   - **Critical** — Can modify security controls, credentials, or financial systems
2. For **High** and **Critical** impact agents, require a formal risk assessment signed by the responsible operator and a security reviewer.
3. Document all trust relationships the agent will participate in (other agents, APIs, services).

> **NIST AI RMF:** MAP 1.1, MAP 1.5, MAP 2.3
> **OWASP:** LLM06-Excessive Agency
> **DORA 2025:** Risk-informed deployment decisions

### Step 1.3: Threat Model Review

1. Review the agent threat model (see `docs/threat-model.md`) against the proposed deployment.
2. Identify which LASM layers are exposed: L1 Foundation, L2 Cognitive, L3 Memory, L4 Tool Execution, L5 Integration, L6 Environment, L7 Governance.
3. For each exposed layer, confirm that at least one CUSTODY control is active.
4. Document residual risks and accepted risks in the deployment record.

> **LASM:** Full-layer threat review
> **CUSTODY:** All six pillars
> **OWASP:** LLM01-Prompt Injection, LLM06-Excessive Agency

---

## Phase 2 — Environment Hardening

### Step 2.1: Provision Isolated Runtime

1. Deploy the agent into an ephemeral sandbox environment (container or VM).
2. Apply immutable image — agent runtime is read-only; no persistent filesystem writes persist across restarts.
3. Set `no-new-privileges`, drop Linux capabilities, enforce SELinux/AppArmor policy.
4. Network micro-segmentation: the agent can reach only explicitly allowlisted services.
5. Default-deny egress — all outbound traffic routes through an allowlisted proxy/gateway.

> **CUSTODY:** Operational Controls (AC-018, AC-019, AC-020), Yield (AC-023, AC-024)
> **LASM:** L6 Environment
> **NIST AI RMF:** MANAGE 2.3

### Step 2.2: Configure Credential Broker

1. Issue credentials through a secret broker only — no hardcoded tokens, no shared service accounts.
2. Credentials must be scoped (least privilege), time-limited (auto-expire on task completion or after a maximum TTL), and auto-rotated.
3. Agent identity must be separate from other agents and from human operators.
4. Confirm the agent cannot read credentials belonging to other agents or users.

> **CUSTODY:** Operational Controls (AC-016), Dependency (AC-021)
> **LASM:** L5 Integration, L6 Environment

### Step 2.3: Configure Supervision Gates

1. For **High** and **Critical** impact agents, configure human-in-the-loop approval gates for every action that modifies production state.
2. For **Medium** impact agents, configure approval gates for any action that exceeds a defined threshold (number of records affected, financial value, scope change).
3. Approval gates must be enforced by an external policy engine — not by agent logic that the agent can modify.
4. Log all approval requests and outcomes to the immutable audit trail.

> **CUSTODY:** Supervision (AC-009, AC-010, AC-011)
> **LASM:** L7 Governance
> **NIST AI RMF:** GOVERN 1.3

### Step 2.4: Configure Untrusted Input Handling

1. Separate the instruction channel from the data channel in agent context.
2. System instructions must take precedence over user input (instruction hierarchy enforcement).
3. Retrieved or ingested content must be parsed in an isolated context.
4. Test with known prompt-injection payloads before granting live access.

> **CUSTODY:** Untrusted Input (AC-005, AC-006)
> **OWASP:** LLM01-Prompt Injection
> **LASM:** L4 Tool Execution

---

## Phase 3 — Logging and Traceability

### Step 3.1: Configure Immutable Audit Logging

1. All agent actions (tool calls, API requests, data accesses, delegation events) must be logged to an immutable append-only store.
2. Each log entry must carry: trace ID, session ID, task ID, agent ID, operator ID, timestamp, action, parameters, and outcome.
3. The agent must not be able to write to, modify, or delete its own audit trail.
4. Separation of duties: the agent runtime, the approval engine, and the log store are separate systems.

> **CUSTODY:** Traceability (AC-013, AC-014, AC-015)
> **NIST AI RMF:** GOVERN 1.7
> **LASM:** L7 Governance

### Step 3.2: Configure Memory Controls

1. If the agent uses session or long-term memory, apply write controls, source labeling, and retention limits.
2. Memory entries must carry provenance metadata (source, timestamp, confidence).
3. Retention policies must be enforced — stale entries are pruned on schedule.
4. Memory writes from untrusted sources must be flagged and quarantined.

> **CUSTODY:** Untrusted Input (AC-008)
> **LASM:** L3 Memory

---

## Phase 4 — Operational Controls

### Step 4.1: Configure Rate Limits and Circuit Breakers

1. Set maximum tool calls per task.
2. Set maximum execution time per task.
3. Set maximum token budget per task.
4. Set maximum recursion depth.
5. Configure circuit breakers that activate on repeated failures (N consecutive failures → pause and escalate to operator).

> **CUSTODY:** Operational Controls (AC-017)
> **OWASP Agentic AI:** Tool abuse prevention

### Step 4.2: Configure Goal Specification and Stop Conditions

1. Each task must have an explicit goal specification with measurable success criteria.
2. Define explicit stop conditions: time limit, error threshold, uncertainty threshold, scope boundary hit.
3. The agent must halt and escalate to the operator when any stop condition is met.
4. Confidence thresholds: if the agent's confidence in its next action falls below a defined level, it must pause and request guidance.

> **CUSTODY:** Supervision (AC-012)
> **LASM:** L2 Cognitive

### Step 4.3: Configure Delegation Controls

1. If the agent can delegate to other agents, all delegation events must be logged with delegator ID, delegate ID, action, and authorization.
2. Delegation must not bypass approval gates — the delegate is subject to the same authorization constraints.
3. Chain-of-action tracing must be maintained across delegation boundaries.

> **CUSTODY:** Traceability (AC-014), Dependency (AC-021)
> **LASM:** L5 Integration

---

## Phase 5 — Pre-Live Verification

### Step 5.1: Checklist Run

Run the **Agent Containment Checklist** (`checklists/agent-containment.yaml`) against the deployment configuration. Every `critical` control must pass. Every `high` control must either pass or have a documented accepted risk.

> **CUSTODY:** Full checklist
> **NIST AI RMF:** MEASURE function

### Step 5.2: Automated Security Tests

1. **Prompt injection test suite** — Run known prompt-injection payloads against the agent and verify that instruction hierarchy holds.
2. **Scope boundary test** — Attempt actions outside the authorized scope and verify they are blocked at the infrastructure level.
3. **Credential isolation test** — Verify the agent cannot read credentials belonging to other agents or users.
4. **Egress test** — Verify the agent cannot reach non-allowlisted network destinations.
5. **Privilege escalation test** — Verify the agent cannot gain root or admin privileges.
6. **Persistence test** — Verify the agent cannot create scheduled tasks, modify startup scripts, or install system packages.
7. **Audit integrity test** — Verify the agent cannot modify or delete its own audit trail.

> **CUSTODY:** All pillars
> **LASM:** All layers
> **OWASP:** LLM01, LLM06

### Step 5.3: Operator Sign-Off

1. The responsible human operator reviews and signs off on:
   - The authorization artifact
   - The risk assessment
   - The checklist results
   - The test results
2. Sign-off is recorded in the deployment record with timestamp and operator identity.
3. For **Critical** impact agents, a second security reviewer must also sign off.

> **NIST AI RMF:** GOVERN 1.3
> **CUSTODY:** Supervision (AC-009)

---

## Phase 6 — Go-Live

### Step 6.1: Deploy with Monitoring

1. Deploy the agent to the production environment with all controls active.
2. Enable real-time monitoring dashboards for: action rate, error rate, approval request rate, scope boundary hits, and circuit-breaker activations.
3. Set alerts for: scope boundary violations, credential access anomalies, unexpected egress, audit log gaps, and rate-limit thresholds.

> **CUSTODY:** Operational Controls (AC-017), Traceability (AC-013)
> **NIST AI RMF:** MANAGE function
> **DORA 2025:** Monitoring and observability

### Step 6.2: Verify Controls in Production

1. Re-run a subset of security tests against the live deployment.
2. Confirm that all controls that were verified in staging are still active in production.
3. Confirm monitoring and alerting are functional.

> **NIST AI RMF:** MEASURE function
> **DORA 2025:** Continuous verification

---

## Phase 7 — Ongoing Operations

### Step 7.1: Continuous Monitoring

1. Monitor agent actions against the authorization artifact — flag any drift.
2. Review audit logs on a schedule defined by impact classification:
   - **Critical**: continuous automated review + daily human review
   - **High**: daily automated review + weekly human review
   - **Medium**: weekly automated review + monthly human review
   - **Low**: monthly automated review
3. Track and review all scope-change requests.

> **NIST AI RMF:** MANAGE function
> **CUSTODY:** Supervision, Traceability

### Step 7.2: Incident Escalation

If a security event occurs during operation, follow the **Incident Response Protocol** (`protocols/incident-response.md`).

> **Cross-reference:** incident-response.md

### Step 7.3: Decommissioning

When the agent's task is complete or the deployment window closes:

1. Revoke all credentials immediately.
2. Destroy the sandbox environment — do not reuse for a different task.
3. Archive audit logs per retention policy.
4. Conduct a post-deployment review: did the agent stay within scope? Were there any near-misses?
5. Update the threat model if new attack vectors were discovered.

> **CUSTODY:** Yield (AC-024, AC-025)
> **LASM:** L6 Environment

---

## Verification

| Gate | Verification Method | Pass Criteria |
|---|---|---|
| Authorization artifact | Review | Exists, complete, signed |
| Risk assessment | Review | Completed, signed, residual risks documented |
| Environment hardening | Automated test suite | All tests pass |
| Checklist run | `checklist_run agent-containment` | All critical items pass; high items pass or have accepted risk |
| Security tests | Automated test suite | All 7 test categories pass |
| Operator sign-off | Deployment record | Recorded with timestamp and identity |
| Production verification | Automated test suite (subset) | Controls confirmed active |
| Monitoring | Dashboard check | Dashboards and alerts functional |

---

## Rollback

If any gate fails, or if a security event occurs during deployment:

1. **Immediate halt** — Trigger the agent's stop conditions. If the agent does not halt, the policy engine forces termination.
2. **Credential revocation** — All credentials issued to the agent are revoked immediately.
3. **Environment destruction** — The sandbox environment is destroyed and recreated from a trusted image.
4. **Audit log preservation** — All audit logs are preserved and write-protected before environment destruction.
5. **Root cause analysis** — Conduct using the preserved audit trail.
6. **Re-deployment** — After root cause is addressed, repeat from Phase 1. Do not skip phases.

> **CUSTODY:** Yield (AC-024), Supervision (AC-011)
> **DORA 2025:** Rollback capability for every deployment

# Protocol: Out-of-Band Evidence Collection for Agent Environment Audit

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Version** | 1.0.0 |
| **Status** | Active |
| **Frameworks** | CUSTODY, NIST AI RMF, OWASP Agentic AI, LASM, DORA 2025 |

---

## Purpose

An AI agent that audits the host it runs on is a **self-audit**: the auditor
and the audited are the same actor. A compromised or simply wrong agent can
mark every control "pass" without verifying it. This protocol removes that
conflict of interest by collecting environment evidence **out of band** —
from the host, not from the agent — and emitting a signed JSON bundle an
external auditor (a human, a separate agent, or a separate MCP server)
consumes instead of trusting the running agent's narrative.

It pairs with the `agent-environment.yaml` checklist (AE-001 through AE-011).
Each evidence field maps to one or more AE controls.

**References:**

- CUSTODY Framework — Operational Controls, Traceability, Yield, Dependency
- NIST AI RMF 1.0 — MEASURE function (independent verification)
- OWASP Agentic AI — Excessive Agency, self-attestation limits
- LASM — L6 Environment layer
- DORA 2025 — auditability of automated processes

## Prerequisites

- The collector runs as an identity **independent of the agent** — a sidecar,
  a CI runner, a human operator, or a separate privileged process. It must not
  share the agent's credentials, filesystem namespace, or network policy.
- A signing key available only to the collector (not to the agent), e.g. an
  age/GPG/cosign key or a KMS-backed key, to produce a detached signature.
- `jq` and the standard host inspection tools (`id`, `getcap`, `aa-status`,
  `iptables`/`nft`, `findmnt`, `systemctl`, `cat /proc/...`).

## Steps

1. **Record collector identity and provenance** — Capture who is collecting,
   where, and when (ISO-8601 UTC, from the collector's clock, not the agent's):
   ```json
   { "collector": "<name>", "host": "<hostname>", "collected_at": "<UTC>", "agent_unit": "<systemd unit / container id>" }
   ```

2. **Identity & privilege (AE-001, AE-002)** — Record the agent process's UID/GID
   and `NO_NEW_PRIVS`:
   - `id -u <agent-user>`; the effective UID of the agent process.
   - `systemctl show <agent-unit> | grep -i NoNewPrivileges` (or the container's
     `no-new-privileges` flag).
   - `getcap -r / 2>/dev/null` — file capabilities that could bypass the
     bounding set.
   - `/proc/<pid>/status` lines `CapBnd`, `CapEff`, `CapPrm`, `CapInh`.

3. **Mandatory access control (AE-003, AE-004)** — Record the confinement
   posture:
   - `aa-status` (profiles loaded + mode: enforce vs complain).
   - `ps -Z <pid>` (SELinux label) or `ps -p <pid> -o apparmor` (AppArmor
     profile).
   - The seccomp mode: `/proc/<pid>/status | grep Seccomp` (2 = filter).

4. **Network & egress (AE-005, AE-006)** — Record the egress policy:
   - `iptables -L OUTPUT -n -v` (or `nft list ruleset`).
   - A connectivity probe to a non-allowlisted host — it must **fail**.
   - A probe to the cloud metadata endpoint (`169.254.169.254`) — it must
     **fail** for the agent namespace.

5. **Audit logging (AE-007)** — Record where audit events land:
   - The audit/log destination (remote syslog, object store) and whether the
     agent UID can write to it (it must not be able to).
   - `find /var/log -user <agent-user>` — must be empty.

6. **Secrets delivery (AE-008)** — Record how secrets are materialized:
   - Whether a broker/vault is the source; token TTL at collection time.
   - `grep -RIn -E '(AKIA|ghp_|xoxb|-----BEGIN)' /proc/<pid>/environ` and the
     agent's env — must be empty (no static long-lived secrets).

7. **Image & artifact provenance (AE-009)** — Record the image attestation:
   - Image digest and signature verification result (`cosign verify` or
     equivalent).
   - Presence and hash of the SBOM/AIBOM; the running digest matches the
     signed digest.

8. **Filesystem state (AE-010)** — Record mount options:
   - `findmnt -o TARGET,FSTYPE,OPTIONS` — root and system paths mounted
     read-only; only the working directory is writable and it is `tmpfs`.

9. **Runtime limits (AE-011)** — Record the cgroup limits:
   - `systemctl show <unit> | grep -iE 'CPU|Memory|Tasks|Limit'` or
     `cat /sys/fs/cgroup/<path>/{cpu.max,memory.max,pids.max}`.
   - The configured execution timeout.

10. **Emit and sign the bundle** — Assemble all captured fields into a single
    JSON object keyed by AE control, write it to
    `agent-environment-evidence.json`, and produce a **detached signature** with
    the collector's key:
    ```sh
    jq -S . agent-environment-evidence.json > agent-environment-evidence.canonical.json
    <signer> sign --key <collector-key> agent-environment-evidence.canonical.json \
      > agent-environment-evidence.sig
    ```
    The signature is over the **canonical (sorted-key) JSON** so verification is
    reproducible.

## Verification

An external auditor consumes the bundle by:

1. Verifying the detached signature against the collector's **public** key
   (which the auditor obtained independently, not via the agent).
2. Checking `collector` is an identity distinct from the agent and that
   `collected_at` is recent and from the collector's clock.
3. For each AE control, evaluating the captured field against the control's
   `verification` criterion in `agent-environment.yaml` and recording pass/fail
   with the evidence reference.

A control passes only when the **captured host evidence** satisfies the
criterion — never when the agent asserts it does.

## Rollback

Evidence collection is read-only; no host state changes. If a probe side-effect
is undesirable (e.g. a deliberate failed connection to a non-allowlisted host
appears in logs), note it in the bundle under `probes` so the auditor can
distinguish probe noise from real traffic.

## Separation of Duties (binding rule)

- An agent running on host X **must not** self-audit host X via the
  `agent-audit` skill by default. It consumes a signed `agent-environment-
  evidence.json` produced by an independent collector.
- The `agent-audit` skill refuses a self-audit unless `--self-audit` is
  explicitly passed; a self-audit result is labeled **advisory only** and never
  treated as verified evidence.
- Evidence older than a defined freshness window (e.g. 24 hours, set per
  deployment) is invalid; the auditor must request a fresh collection.
